system.name: GraphVLM
system.one_liner: A benchmark of three ways to use vision-language models for multimodal graph learning: as encoder, as aligner and as predictor.

content.variant_note: methods hung on a dated axis in three colour-coded family bands, plus a dashed inset with three mini schematics of the VLM roles in the same colours
content.argues: Existing graph learning methods fall into three groups by prediction backbone (GNN, GraphLLM, VLM), and VLMs play a matching role in each group: encoder, aligner, predictor.
content.subject: A timeline of graph learning methods in three families, and three mini schematics of how a VLM is used in each.

lessons.what_to_learn: Place the benchmark design inside a related-work timeline: methods hang off a dated axis in colour-coded family bands, and a dashed inset of mini input-to-output schematics in the same colours says how the new work uses the models of each family.
lessons.suits: Benchmark or survey papers that sort prior methods into a few families by backbone and then define the roles or protocols compared; colour keeps families and roles aligned.

evidence: Figure 1 illustrates the overall benchmark design together with a timeline of representative graph learning research.
Existing graph learning methods are categorized into three groups based on the prediction backbone.

summary: GraphVLM is a benchmark for how vision-language models can serve multimodal graph learning, where nodes carry images and text. Figure 1 sets the benchmark inside a timeline of graph learning research. A black axis with grey year chips from 2016 to 2025 sends grey arrows up to GNN-based methods in a green band, and down to GraphLLM methods in a blue band and VLM models in an orange band, grouped by prediction backbone. A dashed purple box at the bottom left draws the three VLM roles in the same three colours: VLM-as-Encoder, VLM-as-Aligner and VLM-as-Predictor, each a mini schematic from an input box to an output box with a small sample photo.
